scenes.heading: Samples and populations
scenes.sub: How can 1000 people speak for millions?
scenes.say: News reports say things like fifty-two percent of voters support a plan. But nobody asked every voter. They asked a sample. Let's learn to choose a fair one.
scenes.caption: News reports say things like 52% of voters support a plan. But nobody asked every voter. They asked a sample. Let's learn to choose a fair one.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Stir a pot of soup, then taste one spoonful
scenes.science: Choose a random sample, then use it to judge the whole population
scenes.breaks: Stirred soup is the same all through. People differ, so samples need many people and still vary.
scenes.say: To check soup, you stir it and taste one spoonful. Skim only the oily top and you get the wrong idea. Choosing at random is like stirring. But people aren't all the same like soup, so a sample needs lots of people, and two samples will still differ a little.

scenes.heading: Census or sample?
scenes.say: A census collects data from every member of the population, so it's exact but slow and expensive. A sample uses only part of the population. It's quicker, but it only gives an estimate.

scenes.heading: Ways to choose a sample
points: Simple random: everyone has the same chance
Systematic: random start, then every kth
Stratified: groups in proportion to size
scenes.say: In a simple random sample, everyone has the same chance. A systematic sample picks a random start, then every tenth name, say. A stratified sample takes each group in proportion to its size. A convenience sample asks whoever is handy, and is often biased.

scenes.heading: Systematic sample: every 8th person
scenes.say: Here are forty people, numbered one to forty. We want a sample of five, so the step is forty divided by five, which is eight. We pick a random start, three, then shade every eighth person: eleven, nineteen, twenty-seven and thirty-five.
scenes.caption: 40 people, sample of 5: step = 40 ÷ 5 = 8. Random start at 3, then 11, 19, 27 and 35.

scenes.heading: Stratified sample
scenes.question: 360 Year 7, 300 Year 8 and 240 Year 9 students. Choose a stratified sample of 45.
scenes.say: A school has three hundred and sixty Year sevens, three hundred Year eights and two hundred and forty Year nines. That's nine hundred altogether. For a sample of forty-five, Year seven gets three sixty over nine hundred times forty-five, which is eighteen. Year eight gets fifteen and Year nine gets twelve. They add to forty-five.
scenes.caption: A school has 360 Year 7s, 300 Year 8s and 240 Year 9s. That's 900 altogether. For a sample of 45, Year 7 gets 360/900 × 45 = 18. Year 8 gets 15 and Year 9 gets 12. They add to 45.

scenes.heading: Estimating from a sample
parts: part of the sample with the feature
scenes.say: To estimate for the whole population, take the fraction of the sample with the feature and multiply by the population size.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: In a random sample of 60 students from a school of 840, 21 catch a bus. Estimate the number who catch a bus.
lines: Assume the same for the whole school
scenes.say: In a random sample of sixty students, twenty-one catch a bus. That's twenty-one over sixty, or zero point three five. Assume the whole school of eight hundred and forty is the same. Zero point three five times eight hundred and forty is two hundred and ninety-four students.
scenes.caption: In a random sample of 60 students, 21 catch a bus. That's 21/60, or 0.35. Assume the whole school of 840 is the same. 0.35 × 840 = 294 students.

points: Random choosing makes a sample fair
Bigger samples vary less, but bias stays
scenes.say: Quick recap. A census asks everyone; a sample asks some. Choose samples randomly to keep them fair. Bigger samples vary less, but they don't fix bias. And estimate by multiplying the sample fraction by the population. Now try the practice questions!
